For scores s⁺ and descending negative scores n₁≥…≥n₉₉, define m₁=s⁺−n₁ and m₁₀=s⁺−n₁₀. Directly from ranking: absent ties, m₁>0 identifies rank 1, whereas m₁₀>0 exactly identifies an HR@10 hit. A negative m₁ can therefore coexist with successful top-10 retrieval. Track m₁₀ signs, near-zero cases and hit/miss transitions; retain m₁ as a stricter diagnostic. Ties require the evaluator’s actual tie rule. Margin magnitude depends on score scale, so larger average margins across models need not mean higher HR@10.

For paired comparisons, keep users, histories and sampled candidates identical; compare per-user hit differences and report gains/losses plus uncertainty. A practical choice is a paired bootstrap within each category, recomputing the four-category macro difference, or a paired randomization test. These quantify uncertainty for a prespecified comparison, conditional on the candidate draws; they do not establish full-catalog superiority. [Ranking significance studies](https://ciir-publications.cs.umass.edu/getpdf.php?id=744) support paired testing. [Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) show sampled metrics can reverse model ordering even in expectation; recommend full-catalog evaluation where feasible, otherwise corrected estimators with additional assumptions and variance. Preserve this benchmark’s pinned evaluator and describe its result as sampled HR@10.

Repeatedly selecting architectures, checkpoints or hypotheses using the same validation feedback introduces adaptive selection bias; the winning validation score is optimistic. Fixed seeds improve comparability but do not remove that bias. Log all trials, treat validation gains as exploratory, and reserve the untouched host test for final assessment. Ordinary paired confidence intervals do not correct adaptive search. [Dwork et al.](https://research.google/blog/the-reusable-holdout-preserving-validity-in-adaptive-data-analysis/) explain why ordinary holdouts lose validity under adaptive reuse.
